# sysutils_sysctl (Resource)

Manages a kernel parameter, like `sysctl -w`, and optionally persists it in a `sysctl.d` file so that it is set again at boot. The value is written to and read back from `/proc/sys`. On destroy the entry is removed from the `sysctl.d` file; the running kernel keeps its current value. Requires root privileges.

It covers the same ground as `sysctl -w` together with a `sysctl.d` entry, or Ansible's `sysctl` module.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Route packets between interfaces, now and after every reboot. The entry
# goes to /etc/sysctl.d/99-terraform.conf.
resource "sysutils_sysctl" "ip_forward" {
  name  = "net.ipv4.ip_forward"
  value = "1"
}

# A multi-value parameter, persisted in a file of its own.
resource "sysutils_sysctl" "port_range" {
  name  = "net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range"
  value = "1024 65535"
  file  = "/etc/sysctl.d/60-ports.conf"
}

# A per-interface parameter. The "/" stands for the "." in the name of the
# VLAN interface eth0.100.
resource "sysutils_sysctl" "vlan_rp_filter" {
  name  = "net.ipv4.conf.eth0/100.rp_filter"
  value = "2"
}

# Only for the running kernel; nothing is persisted.
resource "sysutils_sysctl" "swappiness" {
  name    = "vm.swappiness"
  value   = "10"
  persist = false
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) The parameter in the dotted form of `sysctl(8)`, such as `"net.ipv4.ip_forward"`. As in `sysctl(8)`, a `/` stands for a `.` inside a component, so the VLAN interface `eth0.100` is written `"net.ipv4.conf.eth0/100.forwarding"`. Only letters, digits and `_-.@+/` are allowed, and no component may be empty or `..`, so the name always refers to a file below `/proc/sys`. Changing this forces a new resource.
- `value` (String) The value to set, such as `"1"` or `"1024 65535"`. Values are compared with runs of white space collapsed, because the kernel separates the fields of multi-value parameters with tabs. Must be a single line without leading or trailing white space.

### Optional

- `file` (String) The `sysctl.d` file to persist the parameter in. It is created if needed and removed again when its last line is removed. Several `sysutils_sysctl` resources can share a file; comments and other entries in it are kept. Must be an absolute path in canonical form. Defaults to `"/etc/sysctl.d/99-terraform.conf"`.
- `persist` (Boolean) Whether to write `<name> = <value>` to `file`, so that `systemd-sysctl` or `sysctl --system` sets the parameter again at boot. If `false`, any entry for `name` is removed from `file` and the value only lasts until the next reboot. Defaults to `true`.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).

## Behavior

### Create

1. The provider refuses to create the resource if `file` already has an entry for `name`. Destroying the resource would remove that entry, so import it instead.
2. The value is written to `/proc/sys/<name with dots as slashes>` with a single write, as `sysctl -w` does, and read back. If the kernel rejects the value, the apply fails. If the kernel reports a different value afterwards, for example because it clamped the value to its limits, the apply fails as well, so that the difference does not show up as a permanent diff.
3. If `persist` is `true`, the line `<name> = <value>` is added to `file`.

Setting the running value comes first, so a value the kernel rejects is never persisted and applied again at every boot.

### Update

- A changed `value` is written to `/proc/sys` and to `file`.
- `persist = false` removes the entry from `file` and `persist = true` adds it.
- A changed `file` removes the entry from the old file and adds it to the new one.
- Changing `name` replaces the resource.

### Destroy

The entry for `name` is removed from `file`. The running kernel keeps its current value until the next reboot: the provider does not know which value to go back to. To restore a value, apply the resource with that value before destroying it.

## Name Validation

Names must be in the dotted form of `sysctl(8)`, with at least two components, and consist of letters, digits and `_-.@+/`. Every component is mapped to a directory or file below `/proc/sys`; a `/` inside a component stands for a `.`, as in `sysctl(8)`. Empty components and components that would become `.` or `..` are rejected at plan time, so a name can never refer to a file outside `/proc/sys`. At apply time, the file is additionally opened with `openat2(2)` confined below `/proc/sys` without following symlinks.

Wildcards, such as `net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter` in `systemd-sysctl`, are not supported. Use one resource per interface instead.

## The sysctl.d File

`file` is edited like `/etc/fstab` by [`sysutils_mount`](./mount.md): the new file is written to a temporary file next to it and renamed into place, keeping the file's mode, owner, group, ACLs and SELinux label. The edit is abandoned if the file was changed by someone else in the meantime. Several resources can share a file; comments, blank lines and all entries for other parameters stay exactly as they are.

- An entry belongs to the resource when its key is `name`. A leading `-` (ignore errors) and keys in the slash-separated form, such as `net/ipv4/ip_forward`, are recognized. Commented-out entries never match.
- An existing entry with a different value is replaced in place. New entries are appended at the end.
- If the file sets `name` several times, the last one is used at boot. Refresh warns about the extra entries, and the next apply that changes the resource removes them.
- A missing file is created with mode `0644`, along with its parent directory. A file that is left without any lines after an entry is removed is deleted.

The provider does not check whether another `sysctl.d` file that is read later, such as one in `/run/sysctl.d` or one that sorts after `file`, overrides the entry at boot. The default file starts with `99-` so that it sorts after most distribution defaults.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads `/proc/sys` and `file`:

- `value` is read from `/proc/sys`. Runs of white space are collapsed before comparing, because the kernel separates the fields of multi-value parameters such as `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range` with tabs. If the value was changed, for example with `sysctl -w`, the plan shows it, and the next apply sets it again.
- `persist` is `true` if `file` has an entry for `name` whose value is the one last applied. If the entry is missing or has another value, the plan shows `persist` changing to `true`, and the next apply rewrites the entry.
- If the kernel no longer has the parameter, for example because the module providing it was unloaded or its network interface removed, the resource is removed from the state, and the next apply tries to create it again.

## Import

An existing parameter can be imported by name. If it is persisted in a file other than `/etc/sysctl.d/99-terraform.conf`, append `:` and the path of that file:

```shell
# By name, persisted in /etc/sysctl.d/99-terraform.conf.
terraform import sysutils_sysctl.ip_forward net.ipv4.ip_forward

# By name and the sysctl.d file it is persisted in.
terraform import sysutils_sysctl.port_range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range:/etc/sysctl.d/60-ports.conf
```

`value` is read from `/proc/sys`. `persist` is `true` if the file has an entry for the parameter with the running value.

## Caveats

- The resource requires root. Parameters of the network namespace, such as most of `net.*`, apply to the provider's own namespace, which is normally the host's.
- In containers, `/proc/sys` is usually mounted read-only, and only namespaced parameters can be changed even in privileged ones. Setting a parameter then fails with an error that says so.
- The resource does not apply to the directory set with the provider's `root_dir` argument: `/proc/sys` belongs to the running kernel, and `file` is a path on the host.
- Write-only parameters, such as `vm.drop_caches`, cannot be read back and are not supported. Use [`sysutils_exec`](./exec.md) for them.
- The provider does not run `sysctl --system` or `systemd-sysctl`; the running value is set directly.
